import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The Pompeiu problem

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^{N+1}$ be a bounded domain. A **rigid motion** is an isometry of
$\mathbb{R}^{N+1}$ (a composition of translations and rotations), modelled here by an
`AffineIsometryEquiv` of Euclidean space with itself.

The domain $\Omega$ has the **Pompeiu property** if the only continuous function
$f : \mathbb{R}^{N+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\int_{\sigma(\Omega)} f = 0$ for every rigid motion
$\sigma$ is $f \equiv 0$.

The **Pompeiu problem** (Pompeiu's conjecture) asserted that, among bounded simply connected
domains with Lipschitz boundary, the Euclidean ball is the *only* domain that **fails** to have
the Pompeiu property. That a ball fails is classical: radial functions built from Bessel
functions have vanishing integral over every congruent ball. The converse is false. Two
independent proofs of this negative conclusion are referenced below.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeiu_problem)
- [Encyclopedia of Mathematics](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Pompeiu_problem)
- [BST73] Brown, L., Schreiber, B. M. and Taylor, B. A., *Spectral synthesis and the Pompeiu
  problem*, Ann. Inst. Fourier 23 (1973), 125–154. (Proves a ball fails the Pompeiu property;
  for a ball of radius `R` the witness is `f(x) = sin(a x₁)` with `J_{n/2}(a R) = 0`.)
- Zalcman, L., *A bibliographic survey of the Pompeiu problem*, in Approximation by
  Solutions of Partial Differential Equations, NATO ASI Ser. 365 (1992), 185–194.
- [CLD26] [Cao-Labora, G. and de Dios Pont, J., *Schiffer*](https://github.com/jaumededios/Schiffer),
  a Lean 4 formalization of a non-disk planar counterexample.
- [CS26] Colbrook, M. J. and Stepaniants, G., *A computer-assisted counterexample to the planar
  Pompeiu and Schiffer conjectures*, [arXiv:2608.01579](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01579) (2026).
-/

open MeasureTheory Metric Topology

namespace PompeiuProblem

variable {N : ℕ}

/-- A **rigid motion** of $\mathbb{R}^{N+1}$: an affine isometry of Euclidean space onto itself
(a composition of translations and rotations/reflections). -/
abbrev RigidMotion (N : ℕ) :=
  AffineIsometryEquiv ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1))) (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)))

/-- A set `Ω` has the **Pompeiu property** if the only continuous `f : ℝ^{N+1} → ℝ` whose integral
over every rigid-motion image `σ(Ω)` vanishes is the zero function. -/
def HasPompeiuProperty (Ω : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)))) : Prop :=
  ∀ f : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)) → ℝ, Continuous f →
    (∀ σ : RigidMotion N, (∫ x in Set.image σ Ω, f x) = 0) → ∀ x, f x = 0

/-- `Ω` is a **Euclidean ball**: an open metric ball of positive radius. -/
def IsBall (Ω : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)))) : Prop :=
  ∃ (c : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1))) (r : ℝ), 0 < r ∧ Ω = Metric.ball c r

/-- `Ω` has **Lipschitz boundary** if every boundary point `p` has a neighbourhood `U` in which,
after some rigid motion `σ` (used to choose a "vertical" axis), `Ω` coincides with the strict
subgraph of a Lipschitz function `g` of the first `N` coordinates: a point `x ∈ U` lies in `Ω`
iff its last coordinate (in the `σ`-frame) is below `g` applied to its first `N` coordinates.
This is the standard definition of a Lipschitz domain. -/
def HasLipschitzBoundary (Ω : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)))) : Prop :=
  ∀ p ∈ frontier Ω, ∃ (U : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)))),
    U ∈ 𝓝 p ∧ ∃ (σ : RigidMotion N) (K : NNReal) (g : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N) → ℝ),
      LipschitzWith K g ∧
        ∀ x ∈ U, x ∈ Ω ↔ (σ x) (Fin.last N) <
          g ((WithLp.equiv 2 (Fin N → ℝ)).symm (fun i : Fin N => (σ x) i.castSucc))

/-- The domain hypotheses of Pompeiu's problem: `Ω` is bounded, open, connected (a "domain"),
simply connected, and has Lipschitz boundary. -/
structure IsAdmissibleDomain (Ω : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)))) : Prop where
  bounded            : Bornology.IsBounded Ω
  isOpen             : IsOpen Ω
  connected          : IsConnected Ω
  simplyConnected    : SimplyConnectedSpace Ω
  lipschitzBoundary  : HasLipschitzBoundary Ω

/--
**Pompeiu's conjecture is false.** There is a bounded, simply connected Lipschitz domain in
$\mathbb{R}^2$ which fails to have the Pompeiu property but is not a Euclidean ball. This conclusion
has two independent proofs: the Lean-formalized construction of Cao-Labora and de Dios Pont
[CLD26], and the computer-assisted construction of Colbrook and Stepaniants [CS26].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 42,
  formal_proof using lean4 at
    "https://github.com/jaumededios/Schiffer/blob/2938e277969c329caf154e48a3d8823f3635c7f1/Schiffer/FormalConjecturesSolution.lean#L446-L469"]
theorem pompeiu_conjecture :
    ¬ ∀ (N : ℕ) (Ω : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)))),
      IsAdmissibleDomain Ω → (¬ HasPompeiuProperty Ω ↔ IsBall Ω) := by
  sorry

/--
The classical (easy) direction, proved by Brown–Schreiber–Taylor [BST73]: a Euclidean ball fails
to have the Pompeiu property. For a ball of radius `R`, an explicit witness is `f(x) = sin(a x₁)`
where `a > 0` is chosen so that the Bessel function `J_{n/2}(a R) = 0`; its integral over every
congruent ball vanishes.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 42]
theorem ball_not_hasPompeiuProperty (Ω : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1))))
    (hball : IsBall Ω) :
    ¬ HasPompeiuProperty Ω := by
  sorry

/--
The hard direction of the Pompeiu problem is false: some admissible planar domain lacks the
Pompeiu property without being a ball. Two independent proofs are given in [CLD26] and [CS26].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 42,
  formal_proof using lean4 at
    "https://github.com/jaumededios/Schiffer/blob/2938e277969c329caf154e48a3d8823f3635c7f1/Schiffer/FormalConjecturesSolution.lean#L446-L469"]
theorem not_hasPompeiuProperty_imp_ball :
    ¬ ∀ (N : ℕ) (Ω : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)))),
      IsAdmissibleDomain Ω → ¬ HasPompeiuProperty Ω → IsBall Ω := by
  sorry

/-- Sanity check: the zero function always integrates to `0` over every rigid-motion image, so the
hypothesis in `HasPompeiuProperty` is satisfiable (the property is not vacuously false). -/
@[category test, AMS 42]
theorem integral_zero_eq_zero (Ω : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (N + 1)))) (σ : RigidMotion N) :
    (∫ _x in Set.image σ Ω, (0 : ℝ)) = 0 := by
  simp

end PompeiuProblem

findings.description: The all-dimensional use of `SimplyConnectedSpace Ω` does not impose the connected-exterior condition in the cited higher-dimensional formulation. At `N = 2`, a spherical shell Ω = {x ∈ ℝ³ : a < ‖x‖ < b} satisfies every field of this structure: it is bounded, open, connected, simply connected, and has smooth boundary. Choose a < b to be positive zeros of sin(r) − r cos(r). Then Ω is not a ball and f(x) = sin(x₁) integrates to zero over every rigid copy, by subtracting the corresponding ball integrals. Consequently, both negated all-dimensional theorems admit this classical example and do not require the planar counterexample described in their docstrings. Wikipedia's introductory wording does literally support the chosen simply-connected hypothesis, so this is a material source-scope concern rather than an unqualified misformalization.
findings.source_evidence: The Encyclopedia of Mathematics, https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Pompeiu_problem, requires that ℝⁿ \ closure(Ω) be connected in its higher-dimensional formulation. The linked Szeged description, https://www.math.u-szeged.hu/~odor/pompeiu.htm, requires connected Lipschitz boundary. Williams, 'A partial solution of the Pompeiu problem' (1976), p. 184, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01360881, explicitly constructs non-Pompeiu regions by removing balls whose radii have common Bessel-zero frequencies from a larger such ball. In contrast, CS26 Theorem 1.1 and the CLD26 construction give counterexamples specifically in ℝ². Wikipedia's introduction says 'a simply connected Lipschitz domain' in 'a Euclidean space', explaining the ambiguity.
findings.suggested_fix: Clarify the intended formulation. To state the planar refutation advertised by the theorem docstrings, fix `N := 1` in both negative theorems, or state an explicit existential counterexample in `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)`. For an all-dimensional formulation following the Encyclopedia of Mathematics, use the connected-exterior hypothesis rather than treating simple connectedness as its substitute, with the appropriate dimension restriction.

findings.description: The module docstring at lines 22–24 describes the modeled isometries as compositions of translations and rotations. Such compositions preserve orientation, whereas `RigidMotion` uses all `AffineIsometryEquiv`s and therefore includes reflections. The declaration's own docstring correctly says rotations/reflections; only the module-level description needs correction.
findings.source_evidence: CS26, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01579, proof of the Fourier-circle criterion, explicitly writes a rigid motion as σ(x) = Qx + b with Q ∈ O(2). Williams (1976), p. 183, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01360881, explicitly distinguishes the translations-and-rotations group as containing no reflection.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the module-level parenthetical to 'a composition of translations and rotations/reflections', or 'a translation composed with an orthogonal transformation'.

reformulations.difference: The Lean definition uses real-valued functions, whereas several sources use complex-valued continuous functions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: On every bounded rigid-motion image, a globally continuous function is integrable. A complex function with vanishing integrals has real and imaginary parts with vanishing integrals; if it is nonzero, at least one part is nonzero. Conversely, embed a real witness into ℂ. The bounded-set equivalence was proved in `Review.real_iff_complex` in the scratch file, without using the file's sorry theorems.

reformulations.difference: The file integrates over the open domain Ω, while the Encyclopedia of Mathematics and Zalcman's compact-set formulation use its closure.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a bounded Lipschitz domain, the boundary is covered by finitely many rotated Lipschitz graphs and therefore has Lebesgue measure zero. Ω and its closure consequently have identical integrals, as do all their rigid-motion images. Thus the open-domain and compact-closure formulations agree on the domains used here.

reformulations.difference: The graphing function is required to be globally Lipschitz on the horizontal Euclidean space, rather than Lipschitz only on a local horizontal neighborhood.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A real-valued Lipschitz function on a subset extends to the whole metric space with the same Lipschitz constant. Applying `LipschitzOnWith.extend_real` preserves all graph equalities on the local chart; restricting a global function proves the converse. This equivalence with a localized graph predicate was proved in `Review.global_iff_local_graph`. The arbitrary neighborhood can also be shrunk to the usual coordinate neighborhood.

reformulations.difference: The theorem negates a ball/Pompeiu biconditional, whereas the conjectured classification is usually phrased as the hard implication from failure of the Pompeiu property to being a ball.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The classical ball direction supplies `IsBall Ω → ¬ HasPompeiuProperty Ω` in every allowed dimension. With that direction fixed, the universal biconditional and universal hard implication are equivalent, as are their negations. `Review.full_neg_iff_hard_neg` proves this equivalence with the ball direction as an explicit hypothesis. This logical equivalence does not resolve the separate dimensional/topological scope concern above.
